flags.detail: Key (A) is correct and the const/volatile reasoning is right, but the explanation collapses two different reasons into one false unifying rule: it says a static member function 'cannot carry const, volatile or virtual, all of which qualify an implicit object parameter they don't have.' const and volatile are genuinely cv-qualifiers on the implicit object parameter's type, so that part is accurate. 'virtual' is not a qualifier on the implicit object parameter at all — it isn't part of the function's type/signature the way cv-qualifiers or ref-qualifiers are, and it plays no role in overload resolution the way const does. The real reason a static member function can't be virtual is that virtual dispatch resolves through a vtable pointer stored in a particular object instance, and a static call has no object instance to dispatch on — a different mechanism than 'qualifying this'. As written, a student could come away believing 'virtual' is a this-qualifier akin to const, which is false and would misinform later reasoning about overload resolution / function types.
flags.suggested: Split the rationale: 'const/volatile are disallowed because they qualify the implicit object parameter, which static member functions don't have; virtual is disallowed for a separate reason — dynamic dispatch requires an actual object instance (a vtable pointer stored in that object) to dispatch on, and a static call has none.'
